questions.question_text: Use one application of the trapezoidal rule to estimate the area of a parkland reserve with parallel offset measurements of $15\text{ m}$ and $25\text{ m}$ separated by a width of $8\text{ m}$.

options.why: Did not divide by 2 when applying the formula ($8 \times (15 + 25)$).
Multiplied the width by the second offset only ($8 \times 25 / 2$) instead of adding both offsets.
Divided by 4 instead of 2 in the trapezoidal formula.
Multiplied $22 \times (16 + 28)$ without halving for the trapezoidal rule.
Used only the larger offset ($28\text{ m}$) multiplied by half the width.
Used the smaller offset for the whole width, calculating $22 \times 16 = 352$, instead of averaging the two offsets.

questions.question_text: Estimate the area of a river frontage using two applications of the trapezoidal rule with strip width $h = 12\text{ m}$ and three offsets $d_f = 15\text{ m}$, $d_m = 24\text{ m}$, and $d_l = 21\text{ m}$.

options.why: Omitted the middle offset from the second strip, calculating $6(15 + 24) + 6 \times 21 = 360$.
Forgot to divide by 2 in each trapezoidal strip calculation.
Used a single application across the full $24\text{ m}$ width with only first and last offsets, calculating $12(15 + 21) = 432$.
Used a single application across the full $32\text{ m}$ width ($16 \times (30 + 36)$).
Multiplied strip width by sum of offsets without halving.
Used the middle offset only once across the entire baseline.

questions.question_text: A paddock with a curved boundary has three perpendicular offsets, in order, of $13\text{ m}$, $19\text{ m}$, and $23\text{ m}$. Consecutive offsets are $9\text{ m}$ apart. What is the estimated area using two applications of the trapezoidal rule?

options.why: Used one application across the full $18\text{ m}$ width, calculating $9(13 + 23) = 324$.
Did not halve either strip calculation, giving $9(13 + 19) + 9(19 + 23) = 666$.
Counted the middle offset only once, calculating $\frac{9}{2}(13 + 19 + 23) = 247.5$.

questions.question_text: When a boundary curves outward (away from the baseline), why does a single application of the trapezoidal rule produce an underestimate of the true area?

options.text: The straight line connecting the offset ends lies beneath the curved boundary, leaving out area.
The straight line connecting the offset ends lies above the curved boundary, adding extra area.
options.why: Confused the outward-curving case with an inward-curving boundary.

options.text: The formula uses the average of the offsets rather than the maximum offset height.
options.why: Misidentified the mathematical reason for the underestimate.

options.text: The perpendicular height is measured incorrectly along the baseline.
options.why: Suggested a measurement error rather than a geometric approximation error.

questions.solution_text:
Because the boundary bulges outward, the straight top edge of the approximating trapezium runs inside (beneath) the curve.
The area between the straight chord and the curve is omitted, resulting in an **underestimate**.

questions.question_text: A water reservoir has a curved boundary and three perpendicular offsets, in order, of $27\text{ m}$, $37\text{ m}$, and $33\text{ m}$. Consecutive offsets are $18\text{ m}$ apart. What is the estimated area using two applications of the trapezoidal rule?

options.why: Used one application across the full $36\text{ m}$ width, calculating $18(27 + 33) = 1080$.
Forgot to divide by two in both strips, calculating $18(27 + 37) + 18(37 + 33) = 2412$.
Counted the middle offset only once, calculating $9(27 + 37 + 33) = 873$.

questions.question_text: Use one application of the trapezoidal rule to estimate the area of a section of land with a curved boundary. Its parallel offsets are $27\text{ m}$ and $41\text{ m}$, separated by a perpendicular distance of $16\text{ m}$.

options.why: Did not divide by two, calculating $16(27 + 41) = 1088$.
Used the smaller offset over the entire width, calculating $16 \times 27 = 432$.
Omitted the first offset, calculating $\frac{16}{2} \times 41 = 328$.

questions.question_text: A lagoon has a curved boundary with three perpendicular offsets, in order, of $7.2\text{ m}$, $10.4\text{ m}$, and $8.6\text{ m}$. Consecutive offsets are $7\text{ m}$ apart. What is the estimated area to the nearest square metre using two applications of the trapezoidal rule?

options.why: Used one application across the full $14\text{ m}$ width, calculating $7(7.2 + 8.6) = 110.6$, then rounding.
Forgot to halve both strip calculations, giving $7(7.2 + 10.4) + 7(10.4 + 8.6) = 256.2$, then rounding.
Counted the middle offset only once, calculating $\frac{7}{2}(7.2 + 10.4 + 8.6) = 91.7$, then rounding.

questions.solution_text:
$A_1 \approx \frac{7}{2}(7.2 + 10.4) = 3.5 \times 17.6 = 61.6\text{ m}^2$
$A_2 \approx \frac{7}{2}(10.4 + 8.6) = 3.5 \times 19 = 66.5\text{ m}^2$
$A \approx 61.6 + 66.5 = 128.1\text{ m}^2$
To the nearest square metre, the estimated area is $128\text{ m}^2$.

questions.question_text: A section of land has a curved boundary and three perpendicular offsets, in order, of $19.4\text{ m}$, $27.6\text{ m}$, and $35.2\text{ m}$. The total perpendicular distance from the first offset to the last is $25\text{ m}$, with the middle offset halfway between them. What is the estimated area to the nearest square metre using two applications of the trapezoidal rule?

options.why: Used one application across the full $25\text{ m}$ width, calculating $\frac{25}{2}(19.4 + 35.2) = 682.5$, then rounding.
Used the total width as each strip width, calculating $\frac{25}{2}(19.4 + 27.6) + \frac{25}{2}(27.6 + 35.2) = 1372.5$, then rounding.
Counted the middle offset only once, calculating $\frac{12.5}{2}(19.4 + 27.6 + 35.2) = 513.75$, then rounding.

questions.solution_text:
$h = \frac{25}{2} = 12.5\text{ m}$
$A_1 \approx \frac{12.5}{2}(19.4 + 27.6) = 6.25 \times 47 = 293.75\text{ m}^2$
$A_2 \approx \frac{12.5}{2}(27.6 + 35.2) = 6.25 \times 62.8 = 392.5\text{ m}^2$
$A \approx 293.75 + 392.5 = 686.25\text{ m}^2$
To the nearest square metre, the estimated area is $686\text{ m}^2$.
